title: Kelsey Plum traded to Mercury; Sparks signal reset after failed contention push
dek: The Los Angeles Sparks traded five-time All-Star guard Kelsey Plum to the Phoenix Mercury on August 2, sending her to a team 13 games out of playoff position in exchange for Monique Akoa Makani, a 2027 first-round pick, and a 2028 second-rounder. Plum has been out since June 21 with a lower left leg injury and her status for the Mercury's next game remains unclear. The Sparks, at 10-17 and on a six-game losing streak, appear unlikely to make the playoffs for a sixth consecutive season.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Five-time All-Star Kelsey Plum, averaging 23.9 points and 6.4 assists in 12 games this season, was traded by the Sparks to the Mercury in a deal completed late Saturday, marking only the fourth All-Star midseason trade in WNBA history.
bottom_line: Watch whether Plum returns before the end of the regular season and how quickly she can impact Phoenix's playoff picture if she does. The trade resets both franchises' trajectories, but the Mercury's path back to contention hinges on a player still recovering from injury and uncommitted to staying beyond this season.
body: The Los Angeles Sparks traded five-time All-Star guard Kelsey Plum to the Phoenix Mercury on August 2, per ESPN's reporting, completing the deal late Saturday night as the WNBA trade deadline approached Sunday. In return, the Sparks received forward Monique Akoa Makani, a 2027 first-round pick, and a 2028 second-rounder. The transaction marks only the fourth time in league history that an All-Star has been traded midseason.

Plum, a two-time WNBA champion, arrived in Los Angeles ahead of the 2025 season in a move that signaled the Sparks' pivot away from a full rebuild toward immediate contention. She led the WNBA in scoring this campaign before a lower left leg injury sidelined her on June 21. In 12 games, Plum averaged 23.9 points and 6.4 assists, both career highs, according to ESPN.

The timing of the trade introduces immediate uncertainty: Plum was expected to return for the Sparks' Sunday matchup against Portland Fire before the deal closed, but her availability for the Mercury's Monday game against Chicago remains unknown, per ESPN's reporting. Plum missed time earlier in the season because of an ankle injury as well.

The Sparks' decision to trade her reflects the collapse of a roster that was constructed to compete now. The team sits at 10-17 with a six-game losing streak and appears unlikely to make the playoffs for a sixth consecutive season, according to ESPN. This trajectory marks a dramatic reversal from the franchise's earlier commitment to a rebuild after drafting Cameron Brink and Rickea Jackson in 2024. The Sparks then traded the No. 2 draft pick for Plum and brought in veterans Nneka Ogwumike and Ariel Atkins (acquiring the latter by trading Jackson) before this season to accelerate their window. That bet has not paid off.

The front-office instability compounds the sense of reset: the Sparks parted ways with general manager Raegan Pebley earlier in August, elevating assistant GMs Zach Knowlton and Nate Nielsen to interim roles. Both are new to the WNBA, according to ESPN. Neither a strong draft position nor a fresh asset haul from the Plum deal appears to guarantee clarity on next steps.

For the Mercury, the acquisition represents a high-stakes gamble on a player's ability to impact a team currently 13 games out of first place and six games behind the eighth-place New York Liberty, per ESPN. The Mercury reached the WNBA Finals last season but sit at 11-19 this year. Plum's own long-term commitment remains in question: according to ESPN, she still intends to go through the full free agency process in the offseason, though remaining with the Mercury is not off the table.

The open questions center on timing and durability. How quickly can Plum return and be effective for Phoenix? And will the Mercury's window for contention remain open if Plum opts elsewhere in free agency after this season?
